new_statements.quote: Word stress (marked ' in this account) is phonemic in Koiari. Although there are no contrasting sets of words distinguished by stress alone in the language the placement of stress does contrast in analogous environments in a few words ('egeka 'long' a'geka 'lightweight') and in others its placement cannot be predicted. [...] For roots of one or two syllables in other word classes stress always falls on the first syllable [...] In roots of three syllables, however, stress falls on the syllable introduced by the second last consonant except where there is no such consonant when the stress falls on the first syllable. [...] In roots of four or more syllables stress falls on the first syllable (as for two-syllable words) as well as on the syllable introduced by the second last consonant

new_statements.rule_in_words: Non-verb roots: 1-2 syllables -> initial stress; 3 syllables -> the syllable that begins with the root's second-last consonant (penult in a'kuba, a'teki, e'moria; initial in 'baeka, and initial by default when there is no second-last consonant: 'aea, 'aefa, 'arai); 4+ syllables -> initial stress plus a stress on the second-last-consonant syllable ('auki'horo, 'avana'deri). Verbs: stress on root-initial syllable and on the syllable containing the second-last consonant of the inflected form (none added with zero 2SG imperative or -e 3SG hortative). Author nonetheless labels stress phonemic because a few items are unpredictable or near-contrastive.
new_statements.secondary_stress: No primary/secondary ranking is stated; roots of four or more syllables and inflected verbs carry two stresses (initial + second-last-consonant syllable), both written with the same mark. Dutton 1969 p.140 likewise: 'utterances of more than three syllables may have more than one stress.'
new_statements.exceptions: Near-pair 'egeka 'long' vs a'geka 'lightweight'; 3-syllable exceptions 'burehe 'ancestor', 'gidoma 'comb'; 4+-syllable exception 'dekui'eku 'backwards'; 'in others its placement cannot be predicted'; dictionary entries mark stress throughout (e.g. akuba with initial stress noted as a variant, line 1319 of text).
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the root/word: 'Excluding verbs this stress pattern is not affected by the addition of suffixes or enclitics' ('yaga > 'yagahe 'at the house', idi 'adaka not *idi a'daka). In sentences 'words are stressed individually' except for shifts under hesitation pauses (pre-pausal syllable stressed and lengthened) and under vowel elision ('ata 'eke > 'a'teke). Stressed vowels are non-phonemically lengthened (p. xi). Isolation (listing) intonation patterns given separately (p. xix).
new_statements.identity_note: Dutton's Koiari data (1969, 1996, 2003) all come from Kailakinumu village in the Laloki headwaters on the eastern edge of the Sogeri Plateau, i.e. the eastern dialect of Koiari (Glottolog 'Grass Koiari' gras1249 = Dutton's 'Koiari'; ISO kbk). The 2003 introduction notes intra-village variation between kin-group lects (Baruari, Haveri, Hogeri, Nidori, Yaritari). Distinct from Koita/Koitabu (koit1244, already catalogued from Dutton 1975) and Mountain Koiali.

sources.note: Appendix 5.83.34 (p.140): 'Stress is phonemic in Koiari. It is symbolized (') where its placement cannot be predicted. Generally the second last syllable of two to four syllable words is stressed, e.g. /'ata/ 'man'; /ma'bara/ 'wife'; /go'roto/.. However the placement of stress is not completely predictable' (examples /ada'hotove/, /'adaka/, /'babaka/, /ba'baika/, /'balahu/, /'gorogo/); placement may vary by environment; utterances of more than three syllables may carry more than one stress. Earlier and shorter than 2003.
